title: Earth’s Interior — Core, Seismic Waves, Mantle and Crust

questions.question: Where is Earth’s core located?
choices: Between the crust and the mantle
Above the mantle but below the crust
questions.explanation: The notes identify the core as the central portion of Earth.

questions.question: Which two parts make up Earth’s core?
choices: The inner core and the outer core
The continental crust and the oceanic crust
questions.explanation: The core has two parts: a solid inner core and a liquid outer core.

questions.question: What is the physical state of Earth’s outer core?
questions.explanation: The outer core is the liquid layer surrounding the inner core.

questions.question: What is the physical state of Earth’s inner core?
questions.explanation: The inner core is solid, even though it is extremely hot.

questions.question: Why does the inner core stay solid despite its high temperature?
choices: It is cooler than Earth’s outer core
The pressure at Earth’s center is very low
questions.explanation: Intense pressure keeps the inner core solid despite the heat.

questions.question: Which metal is a major component of Earth’s core?
questions.explanation: Iron is a major component of the core. The notes also mention sulfur as a possible additional component.

questions.question: What is produced by the movement of conducting liquid in Earth’s outer core?
choices: The heat received from the Sun
questions.explanation: Moving liquid metal in the outer core helps generate Earth’s magnetic field.

questions.question: Which part of Earth is hottest?
questions.explanation: The sketch identifies the innermost solid core as the hottest region and labels the outer core as hot.

questions.question: What does the P in P waves stand for?
questions.explanation: P waves are primary seismic waves.

questions.question: What does the S in S waves stand for?
questions.explanation: S waves are secondary seismic waves. Surface waves are a different category.

questions.question: P and S waves leave an earthquake at the same time and travel along comparable paths through the same solid material. Which arrives first?
choices: They must arrive at the same time
Their order depends only on the size of the earthquake
questions.explanation: P waves travel faster than S waves, so they arrive first under these conditions.

questions.question: Through which states of matter can P waves travel?
choices: Solids and liquids, but not gases
Liquids and gases, but not solids
questions.explanation: The notes state that P waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases.

questions.question: Through which state of matter can S waves travel?
questions.explanation: S waves travel through solids; they do not pass through liquids or gases.

questions.question: What natural event produces the seismic waves used to study Earth’s interior in these notes?
choices: A change in Earth’s magnetic field
The heating of the crust by sunlight
questions.explanation: The diagrams mark an earthquake as the source of waves that travel through Earth.

questions.question: Which observation supports the conclusion that Earth’s outer core is liquid?
choices: S waves cross it faster than P waves
Both P and S waves pass through it unchanged
P waves can pass through it, but S waves cannot
Only S waves can pass through it
questions.explanation: S waves cannot travel through liquid. Their failure to pass through the outer core is important evidence that it is liquid.

questions.question: Which wave type can pass through the liquid outer core on a path toward the inner core?
questions.explanation: P waves can travel through liquid, so liquid in the outer core does not prevent them from traveling toward the inner core.

questions.question: In a laboratory test, both P waves and S waves pass directly through a sample. Which state is consistent with that result?
choices: Either liquid or gas, but not solid
questions.explanation: Both wave types can travel through a solid. A liquid or gas would not transmit S waves.

questions.question: Which measurements can help scientists investigate the core without traveling there?
choices: Only the temperature of ocean water
The paths and arrival times of earthquake waves
Direct rock samples collected from the inner core
The number of visible cracks in surface rocks alone
questions.explanation: The drawings connect wave paths, travel times and Earth’s internal structure. These provide indirect evidence about the core.

questions.question: Where does the mantle lie?
choices: Between the inner core and the outer core
Between the crust and the outer core
questions.explanation: The mantle extends from beneath the crust down to the outer core.

questions.question: Which main layer makes up most of Earth’s volume?
questions.explanation: The mantle occupies roughly four-fifths of Earth’s volume, so it makes up most of the planet by volume.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of Earth’s mass is in the mantle?
questions.explanation: The notes state that the mantle accounts for about 67% of Earth’s mass, or roughly two-thirds.

questions.question: What is the circulation of a fluid called when hotter, less dense material rises and denser material sinks?
questions.explanation: Convection currents are circulating flows: hotter, less dense material rises while denser material sinks, creating a cycle of motion.

questions.question: Which movement produces a convection current?
choices: Hotter, less dense material sinks while denser material rises
Both hotter and cooler material move only downward
Hotter, less dense material rises while denser material sinks
Both hotter and cooler material move only upward
questions.explanation: Rising hotter, less dense material and sinking denser material create circulating motion. Mantle rock can flow very slowly while remaining mostly solid.

questions.question: How do temperature differences help drive convection currents?
choices: They give all material the same density
They allow S waves to pass through liquids
They create density differences that allow material to rise and sink
questions.explanation: Hotter material is less dense and rises; denser material sinks. Together these movements form a circulating current.

questions.question: What does mantle convection help transfer from Earth’s hotter interior toward cooler regions near the crust?
questions.explanation: The illustrated movement carries warmer material toward cooler regions, helping transfer heat through the mantle.

questions.question: Which main layer is outermost in the Earth cross-section sketches?
questions.explanation: The crust is Earth’s thin, hard outer layer, surrounding the mantle.

questions.question: Which pair names the two main types of Earth’s crust?
questions.explanation: The worksheet lists continental crust and oceanic crust under Features of Earth’s Crust.

questions.question: Starting at Earth’s surface and moving toward the center, which order is correct?
choices: Mantle → crust → outer core → inner core
Crust → outer core → mantle → inner core
Crust → mantle → inner core → outer core
Crust → mantle → outer core → inner core
questions.explanation: The crust surrounds the mantle; the mantle surrounds the outer core; and the inner core is at the center.

questions.question: What does it mean to describe mantle rock as plastic or pliable?
choices: It is made of manufactured plastic
It can slowly bend and deform under pressure
It is a gas that fills empty spaces
It cannot change shape under any force
questions.explanation: Plastic or pliable rock can deform slowly; this does not mean that the mantle is a liquid ocean.

questions.question: The asthenosphere is part of which main layer of Earth?
questions.explanation: The notes place the asthenosphere in the upper mantle.

questions.question: What makes up Earth’s rigid lithosphere?
choices: The crust and the liquid outer core
The crust and the stiff uppermost portion of the mantle
questions.explanation: The lithosphere includes the crust and the stiff uppermost mantle, which form a rigid outer layer together.

questions.question: Which two layers meet at the Moho Discontinuity?
choices: The mantle and the outer core
The outer core and the inner core
questions.explanation: The Moho Discontinuity is the boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.

questions.question: Which type of crust supports the continents?
questions.explanation: Continental crust is the crust on which the continents rest.

questions.question: Which type of crust forms the ocean floor?
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is the crust beneath the oceans.

questions.question: What average thickness do the notes give for continental crust?
questions.explanation: The notes give an average continental-crust thickness of 35 km, or about 21.7 miles. Thickness varies from place to place.

questions.question: What average thickness do the notes give for oceanic crust?
questions.explanation: The notes give an average oceanic-crust thickness of 7 km, or about 4.3 miles. This is thinner than the continental average.

questions.question: Which rock is associated with continental crust in the notes?
questions.explanation: The notes associate continental crust with granite. Continental crust has an overall composition similar to granite; it contains other rocks too.

questions.question: Which pair of rocks is associated with oceanic crust in the notes?
questions.explanation: The notes name basalt and gabbro as rocks of oceanic crust.

questions.question: Which borehole is identified in the notes as the deepest human-made hole into Earth?
questions.explanation: The Kola Superdeep Borehole is known for the greatest vertical penetration into Earth’s crust, rather than the longest total drilling path.

questions.question: How does S-wave speed change in more dense material?
questions.explanation: S waves travel faster through more dense material.
